1	\section{Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	This study establishes that the variance structure of LLM evaluation is format-conditional. Across three multiple-choice benchmarks, item selection accounts for 34--38\% of total variance, while on free-form benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH), item, model, and their interactions each contribute 5--24\% with no single dominant source. Model$\times$item interaction (up to 36\%) is the hidden second-largest source: models differ in which items they find difficult, not in overall ability. Our cross-benchmark D-study framework extends the single-benchmark G-theory approach of \citet{mesting2026hidden} to format-conditional comparison and actionable design budgets.
5	
6	The format-conditional structure implies distinct optimization strategies. For multiple-choice benchmarks, item pool composition is the primary reliability lever; varying prompts or seeds contributes negligible variance. For free-form benchmarks, model identity and model$\times$prompt interaction matter as much as item selection, and evaluation protocols should systematically vary both. Across formats, multi-facet designs are 10.0$\times$ more efficient than single-condition designs (55 versus 552 items for $G \geq 0.80$). BF16 and FP16 are interchangeable under binary scoring on single-GPU inference, which eliminates precision as a required control variable. The released D-study calculator enables practitioners to determine the number of items, models, and conditions needed for a target reliability before data collection.
7	
8	Two extensions are planned. Multi-GPU tensor parallelism will test whether precision separability holds under distributed numerical non-associativity. Fine-tuning variance analysis will quantify how adaptation reshapes the item difficulty profiles that drive model$\times$item interaction.

1	Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation results vary across reproductions, but variance sources interact, and their relative importance shifts with the benchmark format. No unified factorial framework exists to decompose these sources simultaneously across benchmarks. We apply Generalizability theory (G-theory) in a crossed design with seven facets across eight models and five benchmarks, totaling 2.3 million evaluation records. The variance structure is format-conditional: on multiple-choice benchmarks, item selection accounts for 34--38\% of total variance, while on free-form benchmarks, item, model, and their interactions each contribute 5--24\% with no single dominant source. Model$\times$item interaction (up to 36\%) is the hidden second-largest component, larger than all methodology main effects combined. Under binary scoring, BF16 and FP16 numerical precisions are functionally interchangeable ($<$0.1\% interaction). Multi-facet designs require 10.0$\times$ fewer items than single-condition designs to reach a generalizability coefficient of 0.80 (55 versus 552 items). We release an open-source G-theory pipeline and Decision study (D-study) budget calculator for evaluation design optimization.

1	\section{Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	This study establishes that the variance structure of LLM evaluation is format-conditional. Across three multiple-choice benchmarks, item selection accounts for 34--38\% of total variance, while on free-form benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH), item, model, and their interactions each contribute 5--24\% with no single dominant source. Model$\times$item interaction (up to 36\%) is the hidden second-largest source: models differ in which items they find difficult, not in overall ability. Our cross-benchmark D-study framework extends the single-benchmark G-theory approach of \citet{mesting2026hidden} to format-conditional comparison and actionable design budgets.
5	
6	The format-conditional structure implies distinct optimization strategies. For multiple-choice benchmarks, item pool composition is the primary reliability lever; varying prompts or seeds contributes negligible variance. For free-form benchmarks, model identity and model$\times$prompt interaction matter as much as item selection, and evaluation protocols should systematically vary both. The multi-facet efficiency gain is itself format-conditional: MC benchmarks show a 10--12$\times$ ratio while FF benchmarks show 21--22$\times$, indicating that single-condition evaluation of reasoning tasks incurs double the reliability penalty. BF16 and FP16 are interchangeable under binary scoring on single-GPU inference, which eliminates precision as a required control variable. The released D-study calculator enables practitioners to determine the number of items, models, and conditions needed for a target reliability before data collection.
7	
8	Two extensions are planned. Multi-GPU tensor parallelism will test whether precision separability holds under distributed numerical non-associativity. Fine-tuning variance analysis will quantify how adaptation reshapes the item difficulty profiles that drive model$\times$item interaction.

We define \emph{item-related variance} as the sum of the item main effect ($\sigma^2_p$) and the model$\times$item interaction ($\sigma^2_{pM}$). The latter captures differential item functioning (DIF): items whose difficulty ranking changes across models \cite[Ch.~4]{brennan2001generalizability}. Because DIF is operationally an item-level property---it reflects model-specific item difficulty profiles rather than a global model ability shift---aggregating $\sigma^2_p + \sigma^2_{pM}$ provides a unified measure of item-driven variance.

Throughout this paper, we use the following notation: $p$ = item, $M$ = model, $\pi$ = numerical precision, $\delta$ = prompt template, $s$ = random seed, $\tau$ = sampling temperature, $o$ = answer ordering, and $\sigma^2_x$ = variance component for source $x$.

tool_args.new_string: Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation results vary across reproductions, but variance sources interact, and their relative importance shifts with the benchmark format. No unified factorial framework exists to decompose these sources simultaneously across benchmarks. We apply Generalizability theory (G-theory) in a crossed design with seven facets across eight open-weight 7--9B parameter models and five benchmarks, totaling 2.3 million evaluation records. Our results suggest a format-associated variance pattern: on multiple-choice benchmarks, item-related variance---item difficulty plus model$\times$item differential item functioning (DIF)---concentrates at 68--72\%, while on free-form benchmarks it disperses to 31--41\%, with no overlap across all five benchmarks. \paragraph{G-theory for ML practitioners.} In ML terms, a G-study is a multi-way ANOVA on evaluation outcomes where each ``facet'' is a design variable (prompt template, random seed, etc.) and variance components quantify each variable's contribution. A D-study is a what-if analysis: given these variance components, how many conditions per facet are needed to achieve a target reliability? The generalizability coefficient $G$ is analogous to a signal-to-noise ratio, where signal is the true item difficulty variance and noise is everything that changes across evaluation conditions. Unlike cross-validation, which assesses generalization to new data, G-theory assesses generalization across \emph{measurement conditions}---the same items evaluated under different prompts, seeds, and models.

Throughout this paper, we use the following notation: $p$ = item, $M$ = model, $\pi$ = numerical precision, $\delta$ = prompt template, $s$ = random seed, $\tau$ = sampling temperature, $o$ = answer ordering, and $\sigma^2_x$ = variance component for source $x$.

\section{Additional Robustness Analyses}
\label{app:robustness}

We report five robustness analyses that verify the stability of the variance decomposition under alternative analytical choices.

\paragraph{Estimator robustness.} We compare Henderson Method~I with restricted maximum likelihood (REML-EM, 500 iterations, practical convergence $\Delta < 0.003$ percentage points). All variance components differ by $<$0.5 percentage points between estimators. The largest discrepancy occurs on the residual component (0.47pp); all substantive components (item, model$\times$item, model) differ by $<$0.3pp. Henderson Method~I is preferred for our balanced designs because it produces unbiased estimates without distributional assumptions \cite[Ch.~12]{brennan2001generalizability}.

\paragraph{CI method comparison.} Bootstrap (1,000 item-level resamples with replacement) and delete-1 jackknife confidence intervals agree closely: width ratios range from 0.96 to 1.04 across all variance components. The agreement indicates that the dependence structure introduced by item-level bootstrap resampling (which creates $\sim$127 unique items per 200-item resample) does not materially distort interval estimates.

\paragraph{Facet specification sensitivity.} Treating temperature and ordering as fixed (rather than random) facets changes $G_\text{item}$ by only 0.37 percentage points (all-random: 0.820 vs.\ fixed temperature+ordering: 0.824). The small difference reflects the negligible temperature$\times$item (0.65\%) and ordering$\times$item (0.54\%) variance shares. The random-facet assumption is therefore robust to facet classification.

\paragraph{Leave-one-model-out (LOMO).} All eight seven-model subsets preserve the item + model$\times$item dominance pattern: item\_id ranges from 36\% to 41\%, and $G_\text{item}$ ranges from 0.877 to 0.889. No single model disproportionately drives the observed variance structure. The consistency of component rankings across all subsets supports the quasi-random model facet assumption (\S\ref{sec:model_facet}).

\paragraph{Null calibration.} We generate 100 Bernoulli-distributed datasets with item difficulties matched to the empirical distribution but no systematic facet effects. The observed-to-null variance ratio is 1.0008, confirming that Henderson Method~I does not introduce systematic bias when applied to binary outcomes. The null simulation also verifies that the item variance share (58.4\%) is not an artifact of the Bernoulli $p(1-p)$ ceiling: the null produces item variance of 0.08\%, three orders of magnitude below the observed value.
